title: Story to Product
context: Grade 4, the closing topic, and it answers the question the opening page asked and never worked out. An adult sees word problems. What the page is actually doing is naming two decisions that a child normally makes in silence: what one thing is worth, and how many of those things there are. Every question in this section has that same shape under the words. A few of them refuse to hand the number over at all and describe it instead, which is a second job to be finished before the first one starts.

writeup.why: Turn a problem written in sentences into a multiplication, work it, and check it by working the same two numbers the other way round.
writeup.look: A short problem across the top with every number liftable, a question row under it, and a bay split into one for each and how many.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Story to Product' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many numbers are still up in the sentences and how many have come down, two numbers side by side in ink, so a number lifted by mistake can be read there without going back over the problem; on the last phase it carries how many rows each of the two workings opened, written in words. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The problem board runs along the top of the working area, 1086 by 130 at 64,202, holding the problem in two or three ordinary sentences set large enough to read across a room, with every number in it drawn as a card 130 by 56 standing proud of its line; a card lifted out leaves its outline behind in the sentence so the sentence stays readable with a gap in it, and pushing the card back closes the outline again. The question row is 1086 by 76 at 64,346 and stays locked, greyed along its edges, until both sides of the bay below hold a card. The bay is 1086 by 130 at 64,436, split down the middle into two halves 530 wide: the left one for the amount that goes with one of them and the right one for how many of them there are, each with an empty landing square 130 by 56 at its centre and its heading printed under the square rather than over it, so a card never covers the words that say what it is for. The digits bay is 420 by 130 and opens in place of the left half on the phase that needs it, a small panel where a description is turned into digits one place at a time, largest place first, with the finished number rising out of it as a fresh card that behaves like any other card on the board. The working area proper is 1086 by 76 at 64,580 and stays locked until the question row holds a whole multiplication and not a number; unlocked, it takes any method from the chapter, a chart of rose partial product rows or a ruled grid, and the product lands in green. The swap and check strip sits at 64,668, closed to a line 1086 by 4 and growing to 1086 by 62 when the product lands: it stands the two workings side by side with their rows plainly unlike each other, the multiplier that made each set of rows named in the margin, and the two totals drawn level on one line; where the totals agree the line closes as a single bar with the word Same printed on it, which is the word the printed page uses. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a product or a built number has to be written, with a thirteenth key that writes the multiplication sign, because the question row wants a whole multiplication and not a pair of numbers standing next to each other. On the third phase a strip of three words, largest, smallest and dozen, sits under the keys, because a description is read out before anybody starts building it. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, the product under the rule is green, a digit carried into the next column is vermilion and is always drawn small above the column it joins, a partial product row made by one place of the multiplier is rose, and a zero holding a place open or a step that is skipped is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, a carry is told by being small and sitting above the rule, and a row is told by the place named in the margin beside it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the problem the child worked, the two numbers it chose still in the bay, and the answer written back into a sentence.

phases.win: both sides of the bay fill and the sentences the two numbers came from light
phases.does: lifts the amount for one thing into one side of the bay and the count into the other
phases.goal: the amount for one thing and the number of things are picked out of the sentences
phases.says: Find the amount for one of them. Now find how many there are. Those two are the whole question.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a shop sells handicraft items at Rs 115 each and sold 220 of them. Which number goes with one item, which one counts the items, and what is the total sale?
phases.feels: the two numbers are obvious from the first reading, and which of them is which turns out to be the whole question
phases.hands: Read the problem aloud and stop at every number, saying what that number counts before going on, then cover the problem over and say the two numbers back from memory with what each counts.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does one of them cost, or hold, or take? Second rung, the phase's: how many of them are there? Third rung: the problem is cut to one sentence at a time with the rest greyed, and every number is named aloud for what it counts as it comes down. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: the question asks how many in all, and in all has meant adding in every chapter up to this one.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers, so a carton packed with 216 bottles and 8 such cartons is handed in as 224.
wrong.screen: the two sentences are read again one at a time with a strip of eight cartons drawn underneath them, every carton the same size and holding the same 216 whether the child likes it or not. The eight are laid out equal and separate and the strip is read back as one amount taken eight times over, which is a multiplication and comes to 1728. Nothing is cleared and the answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the two numbers turn up in the sentences in that order, and swapping two numbers never changes a product, so nothing on the stage objects to it.
wrong.move: fills the two halves of the bay the other way round, putting the count of cartons into the side for the amount that goes with one and the bottles into the side for how many, and the product comes out as 1728 either way.
wrong.screen: both answer sentences are written out under the bay and read back aloud. One of them says that eight cartons hold 1728 bottles between them, which is the problem. The other says that 216 cartons hold 8 bottles each, which is not, although its arithmetic is identical. The two bay headings light in turn while the sentences are read, and neither sentence is marked.

phases.screen: a two sentence problem with its numbers drawn as cards and the bay below it empty
phases.soWhat: Find the amount that goes with one thing and then find how many of those things there are, and check the pair by reading the answer back as a sentence, because the product on its own will not tell you if the two got swapped.
phases.concept: One amount each, and many of them

phases.win: the question row holds the multiplication and the working area unlocks beneath it
phases.does: writes the multiplication into the question row, and only then starts working
phases.goal: the multiplication is written down in full before any digit is multiplied
phases.says: Write the whole thing down before you work any of it out. Deciding and doing are two jobs.
phases.check: A press prints 114 pages a minute and runs for 3698 minutes. Write the multiplication out in full, and only then say what you would work first.
phases.feels: writing it out first feels like a delay, and then the thing you wrote turns out to be the thing you were about to get wrong
phases.hands: Write the multiplication on the line before anything else goes on the paper at all, then turn the problem face down and work only what you wrote.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what are your two numbers? Second rung, the phase's: what goes between them, and what has to be there before the working area will open? Third rung: the two cards are read up out of the bay into the question row by the tool while the child says each of them aloud. The pad stays open and the working area stays locked until the row is whole.

wrong.why: the numbers are up there on the board and multiplying is the thing that has to happen, so writing it out first looks like a step that can be missed.
wrong.move: starts multiplying digits straight out of the sentences, so a number from the wrong sentence gets picked up halfway through and the working cannot be read back afterwards.
wrong.screen: the working area locks again and the question row stands empty above it. The two cards in the bay are read up into the row one at a time with the multiplication sign written between them, and only when the row holds the whole thing does the working area open under it. Nothing already written is taken away.

wrong.why: every blank row in every book so far has wanted an answer written into it.
wrong.move: writes a number into the question row instead of a multiplication, because a blank row that has to be filled before anything else opens looks like the place an answer goes.
wrong.screen: the question row is labelled again under its left hand end and the working area below it is named as the place an answer is allowed to land. The number the child wrote lifts out of the row and drops into the working area where it can stand, and the row fills instead with the two cards from the bay and the sign between them, at which point the working area opens.

phases.screen: the two chosen numbers in the bay with the question row above the working area still empty
phases.soWhat: Deciding what to work out and working it out are two separate jobs, so the whole multiplication goes down in writing before a single digit is multiplied.
phases.concept: Write the multiplication before working it

phases.win: the empty card fills with the number the description named and the digits bay closes
phases.does: works the described number out in the digits bay and brings it back as a card
phases.goal: a number given only in words is turned into digits before it is used
phases.says: That number is described, not printed. Turn the words into digits before you touch it.
phases.check: What is the largest three digit number, what is the smallest three digit number, and what is their product?
phases.feels: a number that is only described does not feel like a number until you have built it, and then it behaves like every other number on the board
phases.hands: Say the description out loud and build the number one place at a time with digit cards on the table, largest place first, before it is allowed anywhere near the sum.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places has the number you are building? Second rung, the phase's: what is the smallest, or the largest, that each of those places may hold? Third rung: the frame is drawn empty with its places named and filled one at a time, largest place first, with the child saying what each place is allowed to take. Nothing is marked.

wrong.why: the smallest digit that can stand at the front of a number is one, because a zero at the front would not be there at all, and once one has been chosen for the first place it gets chosen for the rest of them too.
wrong.move: takes the smallest three digit number to be 111, so the product of the largest and the smallest three digit numbers comes out as 1,10,889 instead of 99,900.
wrong.screen: a three place frame is drawn and filled from the left. The first place takes the smallest digit that can stand there, which is one, and then the frame asks what the second place may hold; a zero is allowed there and is smaller than a one, so in it goes, and so does the third. The frame reads 100, and 999 x 100 is worked beside it to 99,900. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: a dozen is a word for a roundish number of things, and ten is the roundest number there is.
wrong.move: reads a dozen as ten, so 45 trays of a dozen eggs comes out as 450 instead of 540.
wrong.screen: one tray is drawn with its cups counted out, twelve of them, and the tray is copied until 45 of them stand equal and separate on the board. The digits bay writes twelve onto a card and sends it up into the blank in the sentence, and the working reads 12 x 45 = 540 with the tray still drawn beside it.

phases.screen: a problem naming a number by description, with an empty card where that number should be
phases.soWhat: A description is a question of its own, and it is finished and turned into digits before the multiplying starts.
phases.concept: Some numbers are described rather than printed

phases.win: both workings land on one number and the strip closes with the two rows level
phases.does: swaps the two numbers, works it again and stands the two answers level
phases.goal: the same product is worked the other way round and the two answers are read together
phases.says: Now swap the two numbers and work it again. The answer has to come out the same.
phases.check: You have worked 5569 x 98 and have an answer. How would you check it without repeating a single one of the steps you have just done?
phases.feels: the two workings look nothing like one another right down to the last line, and then they land on the same number
phases.hands: Work the product on paper, then turn the page over, swap the two numbers and work it again without looking back, and only then put the two answers side by side.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which two numbers are you multiplying? Second rung, the phase's: which of them was the multiplier, and what happens to the rows when the other one takes its place? Third rung: the swapped working is opened row by row beside the first with the multiplier that made each row named in the margin. Nothing in either working is ever marked right or wrong.

wrong.why: a second go at the same working feels like a second opinion, and it lands on the same number, which feels a great deal like agreement.
wrong.move: checks by working the same product the same way a second time, gets the same answer and calls it checked.
wrong.screen: the two workings are stood side by side and shown to be the same rows in the same order; a slip is put into the first row of both at the same moment and both totals move together, so the two agree with each other and are both wrong. The swapped working is then run beside them with rows that are nothing like theirs, and it does not move. Nothing is marked.

wrong.why: the two workings show a different count of rows and different numbers in every one of them, and difference looks a lot like disagreement.
wrong.move: swaps the two numbers, sees that the second working has nothing in common with the first, decides one of them must be wrong, and hands in the shorter one without finishing it.
wrong.screen: both workings are run all the way to their totals with the multiplier that made each set of rows named in the margin. 98 x 5569 opens four rows, 882 and 5880 and 49,000 and 4,90,000, because its multiplier has four places. 5569 x 98 opens two, 44,552 and 5,01,210, because its multiplier has two. The rows are counted off against the multipliers that made them, and both totals land on 5,45,762 and are drawn level.

phases.screen: a finished product with the swap and check strip open beneath it
phases.soWhat: Swapping the two numbers gives a check made of different steps, so it catches a slip that reading my own working back over would simply agree with.
phases.concept: The other order is a free check

writeup.delight: The last phase, the moment the swap and check strip opens on 98 x 5569. The first working runs down the left of the strip in four rose rows, 882 and 5880 and 49,000 and 4,90,000, one for each place of a four digit multiplier. The second runs down beside it in two, 44,552 and 5,01,210, because the multiplier swapped is only two digits long. Nothing about the two looks alike, not the count of rows, not one row in either of them, not the length of the rule underneath. Then both totals drop onto a single line and read 5,45,762, and the line closes as one bar across the strip. The voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a two sentence problem is printed across the board with each of its numbers standing proud of its line as a card, and the bay below is split in two with both halves empty and both headings printed under their landing squares. On the second the bay already holds its two cards and the question row above the working area is empty and greyed at its edges. On the third the board carries a problem that names a number instead of printing it, so one card up in the sentences is blank, and the digits bay stands open in place of the left half of the bay. On the fourth a finished product is sitting in the working area with the swap and check strip closed to a line beneath it. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first number card up in the sentences on the first three phases, or the closed swap and check strip on the last, gives one slow pulse while the voice says to read it through once. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: A bank of problems in sentences and in described numbers, with the digits bay and the swap strip open and a bay for writing your own. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on finding the amount for one thing, writing the multiplication first, turning a described number into digits and checking by swapping.

observations.why: One side holds what a single thing is worth and the other holds how many of those things there are, and the sentences of the problem say which is which.
observations.soWhat: Choosing the two numbers is a move I make on purpose rather than something that happens quietly while I read.
observations.observe: Both sides of the bay had to hold a card before anything could be multiplied, and the two sides are asking for different things.

observations.why: Swapping two numbers never changes a product, so the arithmetic has no objection to make. Only the sentence does.
observations.soWhat: The sentence at the end is the check on what the two numbers meant, and a number with no sentence round it is not yet an answer.
observations.observe: Filling the two sides the wrong way round gave exactly the same product and an answer sentence that described nothing at all.

observations.why: The largest three digit number is 999 and the smallest is 100, and neither of them is printed anywhere in the problem.
observations.soWhat: A description is a question of its own, and I finish it before any multiplying starts.
observations.observe: A number that was only described stayed as a blank card until it had been built in the digits bay.

observations.why: The number of rows is set by however many places the multiplier has, and swapping changes which of the two numbers is the multiplier without changing the product.
observations.soWhat: The other order is a check made of different steps, so it catches a slip that reading my own working back would simply agree with.
observations.observe: 98 x 5569 opened four rows, 5569 x 98 opened two, and both landed on 5,45,762.

source_tool.description: A short problem sits across the top of the stage in ordinary sentences, with every number in it drawn as a card that can be lifted out and pushed back. Under it is a question row, and under that a bay split in two, one side labelled for the amount that goes with a single thing and the other for how many of those things there are. Nothing can be multiplied until both sides of the bay are filled, so choosing the two numbers is a move a child makes rather than something that happens silently. The question row then takes the whole multiplication in writing, and only when it is written does the working area unlock, which keeps deciding and doing apart. Some problems name a number instead of printing it, and for those a digits bay opens where the largest three digit number, or a dozen, or the smallest two digit number is worked out first and comes back as a card that can be lifted like any other. When the product lands, a swap and check strip opens beneath it, works the same two numbers the other way round with different steps, and stands the two answers level so they can be read against each other. The answer is written back into a sentence before the tool will close.
source_tool.art_direction: A problem above a bay in two / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, place cards that split off a multiplier, trays that hold a number while it is taken several times, a table strip that grows a row at a time, and a ruled grid with a diagonal in every cell.

A multiplication set out in columns always shows its columns: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the rows aligned by their right ends, and a horizontal rule between the last row and the product. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach multiplying.
A carried digit is always drawn small, inside a ring above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
A partial product row is drawn with the place of the multiplier that made it named beside it, and with its trailing zeros written rather than implied.

A lattice is drawn as a true grid of equal square cells with one straight diagonal in every cell, all running the same way, the digits of the two numbers sitting outside the grid, and every cell holding two digits on either side of its diagonal even when the pair multiplies to less than ten, so that nothing has to be carried while multiplying.
Where tokens or groups stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn, every group holds the same count, they never overlap, and they stay countable at a glance.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column, a cell or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A digit carried into the next column is vermilion, so it is told apart from the digits it is joining. A partial product row, made by one place of the multiplier, is rose, so a row is read as a part before it is read as an answer. A zero holding a place open, and a place of the multiplier that is skipped, are both grey, because neither one is a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carried digit is told apart by being small and sitting in a ring above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the sentences again with both sides of the bay still showing.
voice.onNext: A new problem. Find what one of them is worth before you touch anything.
voice.opening: Read it through once. What is the question actually asking for?
voice.onFinish: Every problem was written down before it was worked, and every answer went back into a sentence.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Sentences, described numbers, the digits bay and the swap strip all open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: One amount each, and many of them
Write the multiplication before working it
Some numbers are described rather than printed
The other order is a free check

placement.where: After two word problems have been done on paper and at least one has gone wrong for the right reason. The tool is what makes the choosing of the two numbers a visible step, and what keeps the writing down ahead of the working out.

answer_key.rule: Find the amount that goes with one thing, then find how many of those things there are. Those two numbers are the whole question, and one amount repeated once for each thing is a multiplication. Write the multiplication down in full before any of it is worked, because deciding what to work out and working it out are two separate jobs. A number that is described rather than printed, such as the largest three digit number or a dozen, has to be turned into digits first and then used like any other number. Any method from this chapter may be used on the product once it is written. Check by working the same two numbers the other way round, which must give the same answer by different steps, and write the answer back into a sentence.
answer_key.wrong: The numbers go back up into their sentences and the problem is read again one sentence at a time, with the question row still showing and the two sides of the bay left open. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The amount that goes with one day is 145 m, and there are 12 days.
One amount repeated once for each day is a multiplication, so the question is 145 x 12.
145 x 12 = 1740, so the loom weaves 1740 m.
items.question: A loom weaves 145 m of cloth in a day. How much does it weave in 12 days?
items.checkpoint: Find the amount for one thing and how many things there are, and those two are the multiplication.
items.misconception: Adding 145 and 12, because the words how much in all sound like a total to be added.

steps: One carton holds 184 and there are 26 cartons, so write 184 x 26 down before anything is worked.
The ones place of the multiplier gives 184 x 6 = 1104 and the tens place gives 184 x 20 = 3680.
Adding the two partial products gives 4784, so the shop takes 4784 bottles.
items.question: A carton holds 184 bottles and a shop takes 26 cartons. Write the multiplication first, then find the answer.
items.checkpoint: Deciding what to work out and then working it out are two separate jobs.
items.misconception: Starting to multiply digits before the multiplication has been written down, so the wrong pair of numbers gets used.

steps: The largest three digit number is 999, because every one of its places holds the largest digit.
The smallest two digit number is 10, because anything smaller has only one digit.
items.answer: 9990, because the two numbers are 999 and 10
items.question: What is the product of the largest three digit number and the smallest two digit number?
items.checkpoint: A described number has to be turned into digits before anything can be multiplied.
items.misconception: Taking the smallest two digit number to be 0 or 1, neither of which has two digits.

steps: One lamp costs Rs 215 and 124 were sold, so the question is 215 x 124.
Expanding that multiplier gives 215 x 4 = 860, 215 x 20 = 4300 and 215 x 100 = 21,500, which add to 26,660.
The other way round is 124 x 215, which gives 124 x 5 = 620, 124 x 10 = 1240 and 124 x 200 = 24,800, and those add to 26,660 as well.
items.answer: Rs 26,660, and the other order gives Rs 26,660 as well
items.question: A shop sold 124 lamps at Rs 215 each. Find the total, then check it by working the same two numbers the other way round.
items.checkpoint: Working the same product the other way round is a check that uses different steps.
items.misconception: Checking by repeating the same working, which repeats the same slip and agrees with itself.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A bag holds 36 marbles. How many marbles are in 7 such bags?
A weaver takes 150 days to make one shawl. How many days would 9 shawls take?
A bus carries 48 passengers on each trip. Write the multiplication for 15 trips and find the total.
A press prints 126 pages a minute. Write the multiplication for 1450 minutes and find the total.
What is the product of the smallest three digit number and the largest two digit number?
items.final_answer: 9900, because the two numbers are 100 and 99

items.question: A tray holds one dozen eggs. How many eggs are in 45 such trays?
A company assembles 185 scooters an hour. How many in 64 hours? Check your answer the other way round.
items.final_answer: 11,840 scooters, and 64 x 185 comes to 11,840 as well

items.question: A shopkeeper sold 240 carved boxes at Rs 135 each. Find the total sale and check it by swapping the two numbers.
items.final_answer: Rs 32,400, and 135 x 240 comes to Rs 32,400 as well

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: takes a number card out of its sentence and down to the bay
returns a number to its sentence, so nothing is committed
holds the amount that goes with a single thing
holds the number of those things there are
takes the whole multiplication in writing and unlocks the working area
turns a number that is only described into a card of digits
works the same two numbers the other way round and stands the answers level

teaching_notes: Make the question row a real step and do not let anybody past it. A child who has written the multiplication down before working any of it has already done the hard half, and a child who starts multiplying digits straight out of the sentences is guessing. Work the chapter's own printed example together first: a printer that prints 114 pages a minute, running for 3698 minutes, gives three partial products, 14,792 from the ones, 36,980 from the tens and 3,69,800 from the hundreds, which add to 4,21,572 pages. Then go back to the very first page of the chapter, because that is what the linking box asks for. One saree takes 180 days and there are 112 of them, so the total the book asked for on its opening page and never printed is 20,160 days. Have the class work it, then work it the other way round, and let the two answers stand together. The swap and check strip is the habit worth leaving them with. It costs one more working and it catches the slips that reading your own working over never does, because the second route uses different steps. Finish every problem with the answer read aloud as a sentence. A number with no sentence round it is not yet an answer.
generation_prompt: Build a word problem tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A short problem in ordinary sentences sits across the top with every number in it drawn as a liftable card that drags down and pushes back up. Below it a question row waits empty, and below that a bay split in two, one side labelled for the amount that goes with a single thing and the other for how many of those things there are. The question row stays locked until both sides of the bay hold a card, and the working area below stays locked until the whole multiplication has been written into the question row, so choosing and writing both happen before any digit is multiplied. A digits bay opens for problems that describe a number instead of printing it, works the description out in its own small panel and sends the result up as a new card that behaves like any other. The working area takes any method from the chapter, with place rows or a grid. When the product lands, a swap and check strip opens beneath it, works the same two numbers in the other order with visibly different steps, and stands the two answers level for comparison. An answer sentence control writes the finished product back into a sentence before the tool will close. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read the problem and find the amount that goes with one thing, then how many of those things there are. Lift them into the two sides of the bay. Write the whole multiplication into the question row before you work any of it. If a number is only described, build it in the digits bay first. When you have an answer, swap the two numbers and work it again.
